recipe.history:
The leek — Allium ampeloprasum var. porrum — is one of the oldest vegetables in continuous human cultivation, with a history of use stretching back at least four thousand years across the ancient Near East and Mediterranean. Leeks were a dietary staple of ancient Egypt, where they were depicted in tomb paintings alongside onions and garlic as essential provisions for workers building the pyramids; some accounts suggest leeks were so valuable that they were used as currency in parts of the ancient world. The ancient Greeks and Romans prized leeks for their milder, sweeter flavor compared to onions, and the Roman Emperor Nero reportedly consumed leek soup daily to improve his singing voice. In Wales, the leek holds a singular cultural status as one of the national symbols of the country, worn by Welsh soldiers in their caps since at least the time of Henry V and displayed on St. David's Day every March 1st. The origin of the Welsh leek tradition is lost to legend — one story credits it to a 7th-century battle against the Saxons fought in a leek field — but the association of Wales with the leek is among the most enduring in European culinary culture. In France, the leek stars in vichyssoise, the elegant cold leek-and-potato soup; in Scotland, it appears in cock-a-leekie, a broth of chicken and leeks; throughout the British Isles and northern Europe, the leek is a foundational aromatic in soups, braises, and tarts.

Leeks made their way into American cooking through European immigration and the general adoption of French and British culinary techniques in the 19th and 20th centuries. They were never as ubiquitous in American home kitchens as onions or celery, partly due to their relative expense and the labor involved in cleaning their grit-laden layers. But in restaurant kitchens and among serious home cooks, leeks were understood as a superior aromatic — milder than onion, silkier when cooked, with a delicate sweetness that deepened with slow cooking or charring. The farm-to-table movement of the late 20th and early 21st centuries helped rehabilitate the leek's profile, as chefs sourced young leeks directly from farms and treated them as a primary ingredient rather than a background aromatic. Charred leeks in particular became a signature preparation: a whole leek placed directly over an open flame or under a broiler, the outer layers burning to black while the interior steam-cooks to a buttery, sweet tenderness. The charred exterior is peeled away to reveal a silky, smoky, profoundly savory leek inside. As a burger topping, charred leek and leek vinaigrette bring sweetness, smokiness, and acidity to cut through the richness of beef.

Leeks hold a special place in my cooking memory because of an afternoon I spent making leek vinaigrette for the first time. I had bought a bunch of spring leeks from a farmers market — slender, delicate, with long green tops still attached — and wasn't entirely sure what to do with them. I cleaned and halved them lengthwise, blanched them in well-salted boiling water until tender, and then made a simple vinaigrette with sherry vinegar, Dijon mustard, and olive oil. I tossed the still-warm leeks in the dressing and let them sit for twenty minutes. What emerged from that twenty-minute rest was something almost uncanny: the vinegar had brightened and concentrated the leek's sweetness, the oil had coated each layer, and the whole thing tasted more intensely of itself than I expected. It was one of those dishes that is almost embarrassingly simple and somehow tastes like a secret. I ate half of it standing at the counter and put the rest in the refrigerator for the next day, when it tasted even better. I have been making leek vinaigrette ever since, and putting it on things — including, and especially, burgers.

The leek vinaigrette in this burger is cool and acidic, and it needs a medium rare patty — cooked to 130–135°F — to make sense. The lightly sweet-tart vinaigrette wants something rich and juicy to lean against, and a medium rare patty provides exactly that. The fat in the beef at that temperature is fluid and expressive, coating the palate and interacting with the acid and oil of the vinaigrette in a way that is genuinely delicious. Pull the temperature up to medium-well and the patty becomes tight and dry, and the vinaigrette slides off it rather than mingling with it. The charred leek's smokiness pairs with the Maillard crust of the patty — both are products of the same kind of high-heat, controlled browning — and together they create a flavor chord that would not be possible if the inside of the patty didn't remain pink and yielding. This is medium rare as architecture.
ingredients: 4 medium leeks, root end trimmed, dark green tops trimmed
2 leeks, white and light green parts only, thinly sliced into rounds
For the cream cheese and chive spread:
Salt and white pepper to taste
1 cup watercress or peppery micro greens
instructions: 1. Make the milk buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk and water with sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture, softened butter, and egg. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Transfer to oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1–1½ hours until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 6 portions, shape into balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash. Bake 18–20 minutes until golden. Cool completely.

3. Make the cream cheese and chive spread: Beat softened cream cheese until smooth. Add chives, lemon juice, lemon zest, salt, and white pepper. Mix until fully combined. Taste and adjust. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Char the leeks: Halve leeks lengthwise and rinse carefully under cold water, spreading the layers to remove any grit. Dry thoroughly. Brush all surfaces with olive oil and season with salt and pepper. Place directly over a gas burner flame on high heat, turning with tongs, until the outer leaves are charred and blackened in spots, 4–5 minutes. Alternatively, cook under a broiler on high, turning once, 5–6 minutes. Peel away and discard the charred outer layer to reveal the sweet, silky, smoky leek inside. Cut charred leeks into 3-inch sections.

5. Make the leek vinaigrette: In a small saucepan, heat 1 tbsp olive oil over medium-low heat. Add sliced leek rounds and cook gently, stirring, 8–10 minutes until completely softened and beginning to melt. Remove from heat and cool to room temperature. In a bowl, whisk together sherry vinegar, Dijon, honey, shallot, parsley, tarragon, salt, and pepper. Slowly whisk in remaining 2 tbsp olive oil to emulsify. Fold in the cooked leek slices. Taste and adjust acid and salt.
6. Form patties: Gently mix ground beef with salt, pepper, and onion powder. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

7. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side. Flip. Add a slice of Gruyère to each. Add butter to pan. Cook 1–2 more minutes, basting with butter. Remove when internal temperature reads 130–135°F for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
8. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet and toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread cream cheese and chive mixture on both cut sides of each bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted cheese on the bottom bun. Lay 2–3 pieces of charred leek across the patty. Spoon a generous amount of leek vinaigrette over the charred leeks. Add a small handful of watercress or micro greens. Garnish with fresh tarragon leaves and flaky sea salt. Cap and serve immediately.
